verdict: OK to lend in Manesar two-wheelers — pursue Tier-2 OEM-linked component and EV-scooter suppliers with tight covenants; avoid single-OEM-dependent and thin-margin EV assemblers.
title: Manesar two-wheelers: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A two-wheeler is a steel frame, an engine or motor, and a few hundred bought-in parts, assembled and pushed through dealers.** In Manesar the lendable layer is the component and sub-assembly supplier feeding OEM plants, plus dealers and service outlets. Cash turns when the OEM schedules, receives, and pays; the supplier funds raw material and wages in between. **Value sits with whoever holds the OEM schedule, not with whoever owns the biggest shed.**

## Where cash and value actually sit
**OEM-linked suppliers run short working-capital cycles because OEMs buy just-in-time and pay promptly; aftermarket and export sellers carry longer cycles** [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the sales split between OEM, aftermarket and export; if aftermarket or export is above half, ask for the receivable-days trend and size the limit to the longer cycle. **Capex is lumpy and tooling-heavy, and pricing power is thin** — ICRA notes high competitive intensity forces high operational efficiency [8]. If the borrower cannot show a pass-through clause on steel and motor prices, ask how a margin dip is absorbed.

## What has changed now
**National output is running hot: IIP NIC 30 is +25.3% YoY and +22.7% Apr-to-date** [D], and Haryana GST is +10.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]. Peer results confirm the volume: Bajaj, TVS and Hero posted strong Q2 with industry sales up 27 percent [4], and Bajaj called its EV business margin-accretive domestically, though still PLI-supported [5]. **The caution is margin, not volume** — Hero's stock fell 3.6% on input-cost inflation and competitive pressure [7]. Bank credit is +27.0% YoY against output +22.7%, a +4.3 pp gap [D], so some of the growth is leverage, not demand. Note the local sources are thin on Manesar specifically; lean on first principles and peers.

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue Tier-2 component makers with two or more OEM customers, and EV-scooter suppliers with a named OEM order.** Avoid single-OEM-dependent units and thin-margin EV assemblers — Moody's notes EV motorcycle capacity still far exceeds demand [3]. Structure against a sanctioned limit tied to drawing power, monthly stock-and-debt statements, and a covenant that promoter contribution stays in. Take stock statements and OEM payment records every month.

## Early warning signs
**Watch receivable days against the OEM's stated payment terms, and inventory days against schedule.** A supplier whose OEM schedule slips but who keeps building stock is the first to crack.

- Monthly stock-and-debt statement plus drawing-power reconciliation (monthly): utilisation above limit for two consecutive months -> freeze further drawdown and re-size.
- OEM payment record and receivable-days trend (monthly): receivable days stretching beyond agreed terms -> ask for the OEM schedule and confirm order book.
- GST returns versus bank turnover (monthly): a widening gap -> call for sales register and query unrecorded sales.
- Input-cost pass-through evidence on steel and motor prices (quarterly): margin dip without a pass-through clause -> reprice or seek promoter support.
